# Tips From School Districts: Making the Case for Modern ERP


November 02, 2026


by Shauna Seaver


##


When districts consider changing fundamental systems and operations, staying the same seems like a logical choice. The costs of change feel high — but it’s easy to overlook the costs of the status quo. Quantifying those costs can help districts justify modernization to decision-makers and the teams who use the systems every day.


At the recent[Association of School Business Officials](https://asbointl.org/) (ASBO) International Conference in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, Tyler Technologies hosted a panel featuring three school district leaders who have modernized their ERP systems:


- Randy Dewey, Finance Director at Nampa School District 131, Idaho
- Mike Vargas, Assistant Superintendent of Finance & Operations at Marquardt School District 15, Illinois
- Christine Vayda, Business Administrator at SAU 14 Epping School District, New Hampshire


They shared the real-life costs and savings before and after changing their software, shedding light on the hidden costs of disjointed data and departments. Read on to learn about their experiences with assessing process inefficiencies, building buy-in for change, modernizing software systems, and achieving measurable ROI through connected technology.


## The Real-World Costs of Outdated or Underutilized ERP Systems


When districts work in disconnected, outdated, or underutilized systems, they tend to have many of the same inefficiencies in common, including:


- Labor time spent on manual processes
- Errors, corrections, and rework
- Poor employee experience, burnout, and turnover
- Decisions made without real-time data
- Custom software integrations and functionality overlap


At SAU 14 Epping School District, Vayda uncovered inefficiencies in their hiring and onboarding process, causing up to 100 additional labor hours each year.


Vayda: “The cost of an inefficient system doesn’t always show up in a line item in your budget. For example, there were a lot of steps involved in hiring new employees at Epping. Paperwork and emails were moving back and forth between the applicant, the administrators, and the SAU — looking for approvals, looking for missing documents, following up on applicants, and finally entering the information manually into our accounting system. There was a lot of labor time, errors, corrections, and disconnected information, and we started to think about the cost of that — and what it would mean for us to move to a more automated system. We estimated an additional hour of labor to track down information and push that paperwork for each new hire, and that could add up to 100 hours of labor per year. I may not be able to put a dollar amount on that time savings, but I can give that time back to the staff to concentrate on other responsibilities.”


In Epping’s case, their existing software had the functionality they needed to automate hiring processes, but the team didn’t know it existed or how to use it. Working with their ERP provider helped them uncover a better approach.


Vayda: “For me, it’s not always buying a new system, but understanding if we’re using the current system to its full potential. We never want to buy software to eliminate a position, but we do want to eliminate unnecessary steps and burnout for our employees. If I can give back 100 hours a year, that’s a real operational savings.”


## How to Assess School Business Processes for Inefficiency


Most districts know the processes they complete manually could be more efficient but may not actively assess them. Knowing where to start can be difficult. At Marquardt School District 15, Vargas began by putting every task, workflow, and disconnected system on paper, then having honest conversations.


Vargas: “As I was training new staff, I realized there was inefficiency in what I was asking of them. We had several separate third-party systems for time sheets, state reporting, and financial forecasting. It was ridiculous to expect them to remember all these logins, formats, and buttons to press. We also had a laundry list of platforms to pay for, and those costs add up very quickly. My recommendation is to pull job descriptions and discuss the more tedious processes. Understand your team’s work and have constructive conversations — don’t put them in the hot seat and make them feel like they’re being interrogated. Work together to find opportunities for efficiency, identify all those third-party systems, and assess if your current ERP system has functionality to consolidate some of those tasks and platforms.”


Building on those conversations, quantifying inefficiencies can help districts understand their impact and establish improvement goals. Some ways to take a process assessment from an abstract estimate to a concrete example include:


1. Conducting a task audit. Write down tasks, either from job descriptions or conversations with team members, to get a full view of daily work. Look for duplicative or burdensome tasks — especially those that result in overtime hours.
2. Calculating the frequency of errors. Count payroll corrections, GL classification changes, and report revisions. Add up the cost or the time to correct them.
3. Adding up the cost of turnover. Count team departures over the last five years and multiply that by the cost to replace them — which can range from 50-200% of their annual salary!
4. Determining compliance risk. List compliance areas managed manually, then assign a probability for noncompliance and the cost of penalties.
5. Estimating strategic opportunity loss. After adding up the hours spent on manual work, determine the time your team could have spent on analysis, planning, and strategy if processes were more automated.


## Making the Case for School ERP Modernization


After assessing manual processes and quantifying inefficiencies, making a business case for software modernization becomes easier. Understanding current processes helps to determine the most viable solution — whether it’s a sweeping change or adding a new module to an existing system. Concrete numbers can help decision-makers see that change can deliver a return on investment.


For many districts, justifying modernization comes down to budget. At Nampa School District 131, Dewey found that an upfront investment has saved money in the long run — and delivered enhanced services.


Dewey: “In Idaho, we rank 50th in terms of per-student funding compared to other states, so we look closely at every dollar we spend. We have to ask whether we can really afford a purchase or whether we really need to do it. If I spend $50,000 on a product, what does that mean for my budget? We never want those purchases to affect our teaching staff or education dollars, so we have to offset those costs internally. One way we’re doing this is by moving all our software to a hosting environment rather than maintaining it on our own servers. When we ran it all ourselves, we found we needed bigger and bigger networks and higher-paid IT staff to keep it running. It wasn’t something we could afford, so the better option was to utilize our software providers’ cloud services. That helps us lower our costs, while giving us access from anywhere and increasing security.”


At SAU 14 Epping School District, Vayda and other decision-makers pair a thoughtful approach to modernization with a deep consideration for users’ everyday realities.


Vayda: “One thing I’ve learned is to resist the urge to be overly eager about new technology. It’s very easy to sit through a demo for a shiny new product and think, ‘Wow, this is really going to solve everything!’ Obviously, everything works great in a demo. But you have to slow down and think about what it can actually do and why you need the product. For me, that means really understanding current processes, the problems with that system, and the steps that have been taken to eliminate inefficiency. Another major factor is who is actually using the system. As a decision-maker, I may think a new product is a great solution, but I might not have to use it every day. It’s important to understand all of the product’s capabilities to really get that return on investment.


At Epping, that has meant focusing on staff training. When you’re buying a new system, it can be really scary if you don’t know what you’re doing, what the product can actually do, and how to make sure you’re using it effectively. We’ve gotten there by talking to vendors, asking really specific questions, and asking them to show us — not just tell us — how and why it will save us time. Because ultimately, the goal isn’t having more technology; it’s having fewer unnecessary processes so we can get our time back.”


## How to Evaluate a New or Expanded School ERP System


As the panelists noted, implementing new software isn’t a decision to take lightly. Evaluating existing software offerings may uncover new functionality and address challenges. Keeping up with software updates and adding capabilities as district needs grow can help keep spending low and benefits high.


If a district’s process assessment determines that a new ERP system is necessary to meet their needs, choosing the right vendor is crucial. At Marquardt School District 15, that meant prioritizing partnership and industry expertise.


Vargas: “In Illinois, we have two major pension systems with their own complex and ever-evolving requirements. When we looked at our previous system, it couldn’t keep up with the changes those pension systems were making. I sat down with our payroll person to go over pension reporting, and I noticed she had to take pieces of information from several different spots to build one report. It was a lot of work, which led to a lot of overtime hours. We asked ourselves, ‘Why isn’t our current system handling all of this?’


When we evaluated a new software platform, it was important to know how the vendor was staying on top of the ever-changing pension system in our state. That challenge doesn’t just apply to my district, but to every client they plan to have in the state of Illinois. As Christine mentioned, having the wherewithal to ask the questions, understand the challenges, and have those conversations is extremely important when you’re evaluating whether to switch to a new system.”


## What to Look For in a New or Expanded School ERP System


When evaluating new or existing software, vendor trust and partnership are key factors, but the right functionality also helps ensure the system can meet district demands. ERP systems that help districts enhance efficiency offer:


- A Single Source of Truth: Data that lives in one place eliminates reentry and reconciliation between systems, delivering real-time accuracy across departments
- Workflow Automation: A truly connected system means data and processes flow without interruption or intervention to move work forward
- Cross-Functional Visibility: When finance teams can see the impact of HR work and leaders can access real-time reporting, decisions are supported with data
- Federal and State Reporting Alignment: Built-in reporting for specific state and federal requirements simplifies report creation and increases accuracy — without data manipulation
- Vendor Consolidation: Modern software can simplify systems, delivering functionality all in one place instead of in piecemeal solutions


## Looking Back: The ROI of School ERP Modernization


For our panelists, the recurring theme for getting the best return on investment after ERP modernization was to work collaboratively with the software vendor. At Nampa School District 131, that meant leveraging their ERP provider’s cloud resources and security expertise, which helped them access a level of service that wasn’t feasible on their own. At SAU 14 Epping School District, that meant looking at the big picture and prioritizing a system that connects their processes.


Vayda: “When thinking about ROI, I think it’s important to consider the total cost of ownership. Buying the newest standalone product isn’t always the best long-term solution. A product might have a low initial price, but then you start using it and realize you have to invest in other functionality to make it work for your process. Then consider those inefficiencies and additional costs Mike mentioned: will you need another login? Will there be another, separate place where your data lives? Will you need more staff training? How will it communicate with your existing software? If we can just add those functionalities within the product we’re already using, that’s usually the best approach. As the saying goes, don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater — don’t throw out a product before you reach out to your vendor to see if there’s functionality you’re not using that could address your challenges. Having an all-in-one system, where everything comes together and everyone knows where the data lives, is sometimes your best move to make.”
